extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants and patent professionals (independent inventors, in-house teams, patent attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for analyzing, drafting, and submitting responses to patent office actions (rejections and objections), including evidence gathering, examiner interviews, formatting, deadlines, and filing procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish objections vs rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand the difference between an objection (procedural/formality issues that must be corrected) and a rejection (substantive reasons the examiner will not approve the claimed invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page explains that rejections relate to substantive issues (ineligible subject matter, lack of novelty, obviousness, indefiniteness) while objections concern formal aspects (e.g., missing description for drawing figures, non-sequential claims, incorrect dependencies, drawing line clarity). Treat them differently when planning your response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize common statutory grounds for rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Know the typical statutory grounds cited in US rejections: Section 101 (ineligible subject matter), Section 102 (not new), Section 103 (obvious), Section 112 (indefinite/written description/enablement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the statutory citation to focus legal arguments and evidence. The article lists these as common causes of substantive refusal and implies tailoring arguments to each statutory basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read and break down the office action letter components
rubrics_metrics.description: Carefully review the office action's components: identification of the application, response instructions, response deadline, attachments (references/IDS), and summary of actions (status of each claim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article recommends checking application number and owner, following explicit response instructions, noting attachments and cited references, and using the Summary of Actions to map which claims are rejected, objected to, confirmed, or canceled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze the reasons for refusal systematically
rubrics_metrics.description: Dissect the office action to identify for each issue: the precise issue identified, the legal basis (statutes and precedents), and the evidence/references used by the examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a checklist or table that records Issue Identified, Legal Basis, and Evidence Used. Understanding these elements enables a focused response strategy and shows where additional evidence or argument is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview the patent examiner when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Schedule and prepare for a discussion with the examiner (often by telephone) to discuss claim rejections/objections and proposed amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare an agenda and list of discussion points, send the agenda and any proposed amendments before the meeting, use the interview to clarify misunderstandings, and record the examiner's interpretations. The article emphasizes using the interview to narrow issues and craft an efficient response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gather and include relevant evidence and arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Compile supportive documents, legal precedents, and expert declarations as needed to refute the examiner's findings or show compliance with requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include substitute specimens, operational data, case law citations, and expert opinions/declarations. Make sure documents are current, relevant, and directly support contested points; reference them clearly in your response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft a structured, lawyer-worthy response
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize the response with an Introduction, Point-by-Point Responses for each issue, and a Conclusion summarizing requests for advancement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each cited issue provide clear, concise responses backed by legal argument and evidence; include any claim amendments or clarifications. The page stresses systematic treatment of each item raised by the examiner to maximize chances of overcoming the refusal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propose and submit claim amendments when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare proposed amendments to claims to address rejections or objections and include them in the response or send them to the examiner before interviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article recommends sending proposed amendments ahead of an examiner interview and using amendments as part of a combined strategy (argument + amendment) to overcome rejections or resolve formal objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meet the response deadline and manage timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Adhere strictly to the office action response deadline (typically six months from mailing date for non-final actions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use calendar alerts or project-management tools to track deadlines; failure to respond timely can lead to abandonment. The page emphasizes that the initial response deadline is typically six months and is non-negotiable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow correct submission procedures and confirm filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit responses using the patent office's electronic filing system (e.g., USPTO Patent Center), ensure any required fees are paid, and retain confirmation of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify that the submission meets technical requirements, confirm payment went through if a filing fee is required, and keep records of confirmations and communications to protect against disputes about timeliness or completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properly format and organize the response document
rubrics_metrics.description: Format the response to enhance readability: clear headings, subheadings, consistent fonts, logical organization, and dedicated sections for each issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tables or bullet lists to summarize points, label attachments and reference them in the body, and follow local patent office formatting standards. A well-structured response helps the examiner navigate arguments and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include and clearly reference supporting documents (e.g., consent agreements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attach all necessary supporting documents, such as consent agreements, specimens, or referenced prior art, and explicitly reference them in the response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consent agreements can address likelihood-of-confusion issues; attachments should be current and directly supportive. Clearly label attachments and cite them in the relevant point-by-point discussion so the examiner can easily find supporting material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-check for accuracy and completeness; seek expert/legal review
rubrics_metrics.description: Before filing, meticulously review the response for errors or omissions and consider having a legal expert perform a final review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Errors or missing arguments/documents can delay prosecution or harm outcomes. Verify all entity details, cross-reference that every office action issue is addressed, and have a patent practitioner check substantive and procedural compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor arguments to prior-art refusals (novelty/obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: When facing prior art-based rejections, explicitly address how cited references do or do not teach the claimed features and why the claim is novel and/or non-obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article recommends going through prior-art citations from the examiner, filling gaps in your prior art search if needed, and constructing comparisons between your claims and the cited references as part of the point-by-point response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a prosecution strategy informed by legal basis and evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulate an overall response strategy based on the analysis of issues, choosing whether to argue, amend, or present evidence (or some combination) for each rejection/objection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page emphasizes that understanding Issue Identified, Legal Basis, and Evidence Used informs whether to rely on argument, amendment, expert declarations, or interviews to resolve each point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer specialized, secure tools over general-purpose LLMs for confidential drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using general-purpose LLMs directly for confidential office action responses because of data-security and confidentiality concerns, and the need for specialized prompt engineering and UI for patent use-cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article argues that proprietary tools (like IP Author) provide zero data retention/confidentiality agreements, have dedicated prompt engineering, and user interfaces tailored to patent workflows — all beneficial compared with generic LLMs.
